articleSummary: Fiocruz secured a USPTO patent for a malaria treatment method using the DAQ compound, targeting drug-resistant Plasmodium falciparum. Granted in March 2026 and valid to September 5, 2041, the approach, developed by Fiocruz’s René Rachou Institute in Minas Gerais, disrupts hemoglobin digestion by the parasite, similar to chloroquine, leading to parasite death. DAQ shows rapid activity in early infection and effectiveness against both chloroquine-sensitive and -resistant P. falciparum strains, with promising results against Plasmodium vivax—the parasite responsible for most malaria cases in Brazil. Although DAQ is not a new molecule (described in the 1960s), Fiocruz researchers led by Antoniana Krettli revived it, identifying a key structural feature: a triple bond in the chemical chain. The compound’s low-cost potential is highlighted for low- and middle-income countries. Collaborations include UCSF, UFAL, PUC-Rio; ongoing work with Unifesp. Next steps: toxicity testing, dose optimization, and formulation development.

articleSummary: May 8, 2026, China’s CDC warns that ticks pose serious health risks during spring outings. Ticks are parasitic mites found nationwide; China has over 100 hard tick species and about 10 soft ticks. They inhabit grass, shrubs, forests, barns, and pastures and feed on mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians; after feeding they swell from sesame seed to bean- or nail-sized. Major diseases include Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome (SFTS) caused by the Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome virus (SFTSV), now a Category B infectious disease in China since 1 Apr 2026. Babesia infection (babesiosis) can be transmitted by ticks, blood transfusion, or organ transplantation, with fever and possible severe illness. Tick-borne encephalitis and viral hemorrhagic fever are also noted. Prevention: wear light-colored long clothing; tuck cuffs; use DEET or picaridin; treat clothing with permethrin; stay on trails; check body and pets after outdoor activities; bathe on return. For bites, remove mouthparts with tweezers after applying alcohol; seek care within 2–30 days if symptoms or mouthparts persist, and inform clinicians of exposure.

articleHeadline: Cúm và đồng nhiễm tại Việt Nam năm 2026: Chiến lược phòng ngừa hiệu quả
articleSummary: Influenza circulates year-round in Vietnam, driven by tropical climate, high humidity, rainfall, rapid urbanization, and dense population, enabling ongoing transmission and co-circulation with dengue, hand-foot-mouth disease, and meningococcal meningitis. From January through May 2026, Vietnam reported nearly 32,000 dengue cases—over twice the prior year—while hand-foot-mouth disease surpassed 25,000 infections, about 93% in children aged 1–5. Meningococcal meningitis cases have emerged across several provinces, with severe progression in some patients. Coinfections worsen outcomes: prior influenza infection can predispose to other invasive infections; about 12.8% of invasive meningococcal disease cases were linked to preceding influenza. Influenza/COVID-19 coinfection also yields rapid deterioration, with nearly one-third hospitalized and about half of those dying. Vaccination is advocated as active protection, with annual influenza vaccines reducing infection risk, severity, and mortality, especially in high-risk groups; vaccine timing is flexible; reinforce hygiene and masks.

articleSummary: Dengue fever risk persists in Vietnam’s Mekong Delta as drought-driven water storage expands. In Đồng bằng sông Cửu Long, households increasingly store rainwater or municipal water in tarps, barrels, gourds and other containers to cope with drought and saltwater intrusion, potentially creating mosquito breeding sites. Aedes aegypti and larvae (lăng quăng) can thrive in uncovered or poorly maintained receptacles such as drums, vases, buckets, tires, and even garden ponds near fruit orchards and rubber plantations. Authorities should intensify education for farmers and homeowners, ensure water storage is sealed and disinfected, and perform regular larval control to prevent outbreaks, especially on islands like Hải Tặc.

articleSummary: Melioidosis (Whitmore's disease) due to Burkholderia pseudomallei was successfully treated in a 50-year-old man from Gia Lai Province, Vietnam, with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 13.6%). Admitted April 1 with high fever, perineal ulcers, and severe pain in the right thigh and leg, he was initially misdiagnosed as a routine skin infection and given antibiotics. Condition worsened until lab confirmation identified Burkholderia pseudomallei. A aggressive surgical debridement, removal of necrotic tissue, irrigation, and drainage were performed. Telemedicine input from specialists at Bach Mai Hospital helped finalize the diagnosis and optimize intensive care. As of May 8, 2026, the patient is recovering and nearing discharge, with a planned six months of continued antibiotic therapy. This single case underscores melioidosis risk in diabetics and the value of rapid, multidisciplinary intervention.

articleSummary: Three deaths have occurred in a hantavirus outbreak on a cruise ship. The World Health Organization confirms Andes virus, a strain common in Argentina and Chile, as the causative agent; it is the only hantavirus with documented human-to-human transmission after close contact. Most hantavirus infections are rodent-borne, transmitted via contact with rats or mice or their urine, droppings and saliva, and can become airborne during cleaning. Globally, WHO estimates 10,000–100,000 cases annually, with severity varying by strain. In the Americas, hantavirus pulmonary syndrome can progress rapidly and carries up to about 50% fatality; in Europe/Asia, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome is more common, with 1–15% CFR. No specific antiviral exists; management is supportive. Prevention emphasizes rodent control and hygiene; contact tracing enables early hospital access. Argentina reported 21 deaths last year among 66 pulmonary cases (32% CFR); Bolivia and Paraguay show rising infections, with higher mortality noted in Brazil and Argentina.

articleSummary: On the mid-Atlantic cruise MV Hondius, hantavirus infection has caused at least three fatalities. Hantavirus Disease is caused by viruses in the Hantaviridae family carried by rodents, especially mice; there is no vaccine or specific treatment. In the Americas, Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS/HCPS) severely affects the lungs, with fever, myalgias, dyspnea, pulmonary edema, and 40% mortality; in Europe and Asia, Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) damages the kidneys, with fever, petechiae, and possible acute renal failure. Transmission mainly occurs via exposure to rodent excreta—urine, feces, saliva—often through inhalation of dust; other routes include contact with wounds or mucous membranes. Incubation is 1–8 weeks, with symptoms appearing 2–4 weeks after exposure. Prevention emphasizes reducing rodent access, avoiding sweeping droppings, and using diluted disinfectants. Return travelers with fever or respiratory symptoms within 45 days should seek medical care. articleSummary: Aspergillosis is a fungal lung infection caused by Aspergillus and is widely underdiagnosed. Through epidemiologic week 47 of 2025, eight American countries reported 229 HCPS cases and 59 deaths (regional case fatality 25.7%), notably Argentina, Brazil, Bolivia, Chile, the United States, Panama, Paraguay, and Uruguay. Andes virus is unique for documented human-to-human transmission in the Southern Cone; other hantaviruses such as Puumala and Dobrava in Europe transmit by rodent excreta with no confirmed person-to-person spread. Transmission is mainly zoonotic via contact with infected rodent urine, droppings, saliva, or contaminated surfaces/food; Andes outbreaks have occurred in Argentina (1996, 2018) and Chile (1997, 2004, 2014). Incubation is typically 1–3 weeks (range 3–45 days); symptoms begin with fever, myalgias, chills, and headache, may include nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, and can progress to severe respiratory distress requiring ICU care. No vaccine or specific antiviral exists; management is supportive.

articleSummary: On MV Hondius, a Dutch luxury cruise ship, hantavirus infection has been confirmed with five cases and three deaths as of May 8, 2026. The vessel carries about 150 passengers and crew from 28 countries, including two Indian crew members, and departed Ushuaia, Argentina on April 1, with plans to reach the Canary Islands, Spain by May 10. The deceased include a 69-year-old Dutch woman, her husband, and a German woman, with investigations ongoing. The World Health Organization notes hantaviruses are typically rodent-borne, and this represents the first documented human-to-human transmission on a cruise ship. Authorities have mandated masks for all onboard and PPE for those in contact with infected individuals. On April 24, 29 passengers disembarked at Saint Helena; authorities are tracing them, while the remaining passengers and crew are under close health surveillance.

articleHeadline: West Africa inaugurates Lassa fever preparedness exercise
articleSummary: May 4-8, 2026, in Cotonou, Benin, a Lassa fever preparedness simulation was inaugurated to strengthen surveillance coordination and response across West Africa. Organized by the U.S. CDC with AFENET, ECOWAS Regional Centre for Surveillance and Disease Control, IANPHI, and Integrated Laboratory Services, the exercise brings together surveillance and laboratory officers from Benin, Mali, Togo, Ghana, Nigeria, Mauritania and Burkina Faso. Sessions assess laboratory systems, infection prevention, risk communication, community engagement, and cross-border health coordination. Led by Dr Kerton Victory, the exercise aims to improve preparedness and rapid coordinated responses to cross-border health threats. Benin’s Health Ministry Secretary General, Dr Ali Chabi, and U.S. diplomat Shane Dixson emphasized regional collaboration and health security, while AFENET’s Dr Herbert Kazoora highlighted alignment with ‘A Healthier Africa’ to strengthen resilient systems for detecting and responding to emerging public health threats. Lassa fever is endemic in parts of West Africa with annual outbreaks.

articleSummary: Three passengers died from hantavirus aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius in the Atlantic Ocean, highlighting a notable outbreak of a longstanding zoonotic virus. Indonesia’s Health Policy Development Agency (BKPK) notes hantavirus infections occur via aerosolized rodent urine, feces, or saliva, or contact with contaminated surfaces, and can present with fever, muscle pain, nausea, and fatigue. Two main syndromes exist: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), common in Asia/Europe and affecting kidneys and vessels; and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), more frequent in the Americas with severe respiratory failure. In Indonesia, Seoul virus (SEOV) carried by Rattus rattus and R. norvegicus is prevalent; urban centers like Jakarta, Bandung, Semarang, and Denpasar have reported cases. Case fatality can reach tens of percent. Vaccines are limited; control relies on rodent population management, sanitation, education, and risk-based surveillance, with diagnosis aided by serology and PCR.

articleSummary: Hanoi’s Department of Health issued an urgent directive to public and private hospitals and the city’s CDC to intensify surveillance and prevention of Hantavirus disease. Citing WHO, from 1 April–4 May 2026 a cluster of severe acute respiratory illness occurred on a cruise ship traveling from Argentina across the South Atlantic. As of 4 May, seven cases were recorded aboard: two confirmed hantavirus infections and five suspected; three deaths; one critically ill; three with mild symptoms. The ship carried 147 people (88 passengers, 59 crew) from 23 nationalities; no Vietnamese among passengers or crew yet. articleSummary: As of May 8, 2026, Quy Hoa Central Dermatology Hospital in Quy Nhon Nam Ward, Gia Lai, Vietnam, treated a severe Whitmore (melioidosis) infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei in a 50-year-old man from Gia Lai. Initial antibiotics failed; blood cultures grew Burkholderia spp., and MRI revealed multiple abscesses from the gluteal region to the hip joint and lumbosacral area. PCR of purulent discharge confirmed melioidosis due to B. pseudomallei. Management included high-dose antibiotics per susceptibility testing, strict glycemic control with insulin, and extensive surgical debridement with drainage of deep abscesses and the hip joint capsule. articleSummary: Malaria-causing Plasmodium falciparum enzyme Falcipain-2 (FP-2) is identified as a druggable target. Indian researchers led by Sampa Biswas at the Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics (now InBOL Salud) pinpointed a specific pocket in FP-2 that binds PEG400, a fragment of a common polymer used in medicines. This pocket is scarcely conserved in human cathepsins, enabling potential selective inhibition. Computational analyses show PEG400 occupancy blocks FP-2's hemoglobin digestion, depriving the parasite of nutrients and preventing replication. The study, not a drug trial, validates a structural mechanism to guide small-molecule inhibitor design. Experiments in lab and clinical validation are required. Malaria remains endemic across Africa, Asia, and Latin America, with hundreds of millions of cases annually and rising drug resistance, underscoring the need for novel targets.

articleSummary: Rabies prevention is urged as Eid al-Adha approaches in Aceh, by Aceh Department of Animal Husbandry. Slaughter should be away from populations and water sources, with cleaning and disinfection afterward. Slaughter under mosque leadership is encouraged for waste management.

articleSummary: Hantavirus has long circulated in Indonesia, with attention reignited by three deaths linked to the Dutch cruise MV Hondius in Cape Verde waters on 3 May. Hantavirus is a zoonotic group carried mainly by rodents and can cause severe respiratory and renal illness depending on the virus. Indonesian research dates to 1984, showing rodent exposure in 0–34% and human exposure in 0–13% over about 35 years, with at least 14 reported acute human infections (not always lab-confirmed). Notable work includes 2011 findings of Seoul virus infection in humans and rats in West Java; 2013 evidence of Seoul virus antibodies and genome segments in rats from Kepulauan Seribu, with genetic links to Vietnam and Singapore. articleHeadline: What Is Hantavirus? Experts Explain the Deadly Rodent Borne Disease - Diaspora Digital Media (DDM News) - Nigeria Breaking News, Africa and World News and Updates
articleSummary: Rodent-borne hantaviruses can cause deadly illnesses in humans. In North and South America, infection may lead to hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), a serious lung-and-heart condition; in Europe and Asia, hantaviruses are linked to haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), mainly kidney and blood vessel damage. Each virus strain is tied to a specific rodent reservoir; Andes virus in parts of South America has the only confirmed limited human-to-human transmission, typically among close relatives. Global data show infections are relatively uncommon but highly dangerous, with thousands of cases reported yearly in parts of Asia and Europe—especially China and South Korea—and rarer but highly lethal in the Americas. Transmission occurs via inhalation of aerosolized rodent urine, saliva, or droppings; risk is higher during cleaning, farming, forestry, or rodent-infested living spaces. Symptoms appear 1–8 weeks post-exposure: fever, headaches, muscle pain, nausea, fatigue; severe cases include breathing difficulties, pulmonary edema, kidney failure, bleeding, or shock. Diagnosis requires lab testing; there is no vaccine or specific cure; treatment is supportive, and early hospital care improves survival. Prevention focuses on rodent-proofing, hygiene, proper food storage, and safe cleaning; health workers should maintain strict infection control.

articleSummary: Tropical leishmaniasis, including the severe visceral form known as kala-azar, was diagnosed in a young Romanian researcher after returning from Central America. The imported case, rare in Europe, underscores transmission by tiny sandflies (phlebotomines). On the left arm, painful lesions progressed to ulcers, with initial tests and biopsies failing to identify the cause. A second biopsy plus advanced molecular analyses confirmed a tropical Latin American parasite. Treatment posed major challenges: European-available drugs were insufficient, requiring therapy imported from Brazil. Romania’s limited routes for rapid molecular diagnostics and access to tropical-disease treatments compounded the difficulty. Ioana Mitrea, a PhD student at USAMV Cluj-Napoca, endured severe pain and a prolonged recovery. The case, published in an international journal, aims to alert clinicians to travel-related exotic infections and the essential role of molecular confirmation for appropriate treatment.

articleSummary: An international cruise-ship–associated cluster of Hantavirus infections reported in April 2026 raises concern. By May 4, seven cases linked to a ship departing Argentina—visiting Antarctic ecosystems including South Georgia, Tristan da Cunha, and Saint Helena—had been identified: 2 PCR-confirmed and 5 suspected, with three deaths. Patients progressed rapidly from fever and abdominal pain to pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and circulatory shock. Andes virus, a Hantavirus shared with the Americas, can transmit between people, though human-to-human spread is rare. Hantaviruses are RNA viruses carried by rodents; infection typically occurs via inhalation of dust contaminated with rodent urine, droppings, or saliva, or through rodent bites. There is no specific antiviral or vaccine; treatment is supportive, including ventilation, dialysis, or ECMO when needed. Vietnam reports no cases yet, but risk exists; authorities urge rodent control, environmental hygiene, and damp-cleaning with gloves and masks. RT-PCR and serology are available in major hospitals.

articleSummary: Jakarta, Indonesia, May 8, 2026 – Ikatan Dokter Anak Indonesia (IDAI) deems measles and diphtheria cases more urgent for government intervention than hantavirus. He argues prevention should prioritize vaccination and protection since many people remain inadequately immunized. He agrees hantavirus warrants vigilance, but can be addressed through efficient, low-cost methods like Clean and Healthy Living Behaviors (PHBS). articleHeadlineTranslated: Is there a vaccine for hantavirus?

articleSummary: Hantaviruses remain globally relevant with an outbreak linked to the MV Hondius caused by Andes virus (ANDV), a hantavirus circulating in South America’s Southern Cone with rare, close-contact person-to-person transmission. articleSummary: Wastewater surveillance in Gujarat's four cities, Ahmedabad, Gandhinagar, Rajkot and Vadodara, over Sep 2023–Sep 2024 identified a broad range of viruses, including SARS-CoV-2, influenza A, RSV, rotavirus, norovirus, and hepatitis A, alongside zoonotic agents such as avian coronavirus and hepatitis E. Substantial inter-city and site variability was observed, with Ahmedabad showing especially high diversity. Viral abundance correlated with digital PCR measurements for SARS-CoV-2 and rotavirus; hepatitis A signals mirrored Gujarat's clinical trends. In Brazil, leptospirosis remains the most prevalent waterborne disease after heavy rains, while hantavirus exposure stays linked to rural environments. Rapid diagnosis and protective measures are crucial.
